title: Pack and Unpack a List of Strings
statement:
You need to send a list of strings through a channel that only carries one string. Design two functions:

  • encode(strs) turns the list into a single string.
  • decode(data) gets only that single string and must rebuild the exact original list.

The strings may contain any character: letters, digits, spaces, newlines, #, commas, emoji, and whatever delimiter you were planning to use. Empty strings and an empty list must survive too, and [] and [""] must come back different.

How it is tested. The runner calls one function, so implement roundTrip(strs): write encode and decode as helpers inside it and return decode(encode(strs)). A test passes when the result equals the input list. Returning strs directly would pass, but it skips the whole exercise: decode must use nothing except the string that encode produced.

examples.why: One possible encoding is "4#save4#load": each string's length, a #, then the string itself.
Joining with "#" would split "a#b" in two. A length prefix works because the decoder reads exactly that many characters, whatever they are.
An empty list must not come back as [""]. Its encoding has to differ from the encoding of one empty string.

constraints: strs[i] may contain any Unicode character
decode may only use the string returned by encode
hints: Any single delimiter character can also appear inside a string. How could the decoder know where a string ends without searching for a special character?
Write down how long each string is before the string itself. Then the decoder reads that many characters blindly, even if they look like delimiters.
The length itself needs an end marker, because lengths have different numbers of digits. Use "length#string" and, when decoding, read digits up to the first # starting from your current position.

explain.intuition:
The problem with a plain delimiter is that the data can contain it. There are two standard fixes, and both show up in real protocols.

Length prefix: write 5#hello. The decoder reads digits up to the first #, then takes exactly that many characters without looking at them. HTTP's Content-Length and many binary formats work this way. Escaping: pick an escape character, double it inside the data, and mark real separators with something the data can never produce, the way JSON escapes " inside strings.
steps: encode: for each string append its length, then #, then the string.
decode: keep a position i. Find the first # at or after i; the digits between are the length len.
Take the len characters right after that # as the next string, then move i past them.
Repeat until i reaches the end. An empty list encodes to "" and decodes to [], while [""] encodes to "0#".
pitfalls: Searching for # from the start of the remaining data after reading a string's length. In "3#a#b" the string is "a#b"; the decoder must skip the 3 characters, not look for the next # inside them.
Using a separator between strings instead of a terminator after each one: then [] and [""] both encode to "".
Assuming lengths are one digit. A 16-character string needs "16#".

solutions.title: Escape and terminate
solutions.idea: Inside each string, write ~ as ~~ and a comma as ~,. Then end every string with a bare comma. A bare comma can only be a terminator, because every comma inside the data is preceded by ~.

solutions.title: Length prefix
solutions.idea: Write each string as length#string. The decoder reads the length, then takes that many characters without inspecting them.

followups: The channel only carries bytes. How does the length prefix change when one character can take several bytes?
Decode a stream that arrives in chunks, where a chunk can end in the middle of a length or a string. What state do you keep between chunks?
